passage:
Dear Farhan,
Nanaji took me around old Lucknow on Sunday. At every haveli he'd tap a wall and say, "See? Two hundred years. Today's buildings won't last twenty." I nodded, because the carved doors really are beautiful.
But as an architect, something kept bugging me. We were only walking past the old buildings that are still standing. What about the ones from the same time that cracked, flooded, or were pulled down a century ago? They're not on the tour. They're parking lots now.
So maybe old builders weren't all better. Maybe we only get to see their best work.
I didn't say this to Nanaji. He was so happy. But I keep wondering which of our buildings people will be admiring two hundred years from now.
Ganga

qa.q: What did Nanaji say at every haveli?
qa.a: See? Two hundred years. Today's buildings won't last twenty.

qa.q: What was Ganga thinking while walking past the havelis?
qa.a: Ganga realised they were only seeing the old buildings still standing, not the ones from the same time that fell or were pulled down.

qa.q: How could Ganga share this idea with Nanaji kindly?
qa.a: Ganga could admire the carved doors with Nanaji and gently ask what happened to buildings from his childhood that are gone.

qa.q: How does Nanaji experience the walk?
qa.a: Nanaji is proud and happy, seeing the standing havelis as proof that the old ways were better.

grounding: A young architect hears that old buildings were better made and notes that only the durable ones are still around to be seen.

passage: My uncle says it every Sunday lunch: "Old songs had soul. Today's songs are noise." And honestly, Ganga, the old playlist he puts on is gorgeous. But here's what I figured out, working at the radio station. I'm Tushar, I handle the archive. We have boxes of records from the sixties, hundreds of film songs nobody has played in forty years. Some are fine, most are forgettable, a few are truly terrible. They never made it into anyone's playlist. So when my uncle compares his top fifty old songs with whatever new song comes on the radio, it's not a fair fight. The weak old ones have already been forgotten. Give today's songs forty years, and the best of them will sound like soul too.

qa.a: Tushar handles the archive.

qa.a: Tushar realised most old songs were forgettable and simply dropped away, and seems amused that only the best reach the uncle's playlist.

qa.q: Why might Tushar's uncle feel so sure old songs were better?
qa.a: The uncle only hears the top fifty that survived, so the old era sounds full of gems next to random new songs.

grounding: A young archivist hears that old songs were better and notes that only the best old songs are still being played.

passage: I'm Pranav, and I was at the office farewell when Mr Rawat started on his favourite topic. "In our time, steel almirahs lasted forty years. Everything today breaks in two." Most of us nodded politely. Vidya, who joined last year as an engineer, smiled and said, "Sir, your almirah lasted. But how many from that factory rusted in five years and went to the kabadiwala?" Mr Rawat laughed. "Those were cheap ones." "Exactly," Vidya said gently. "The cheap ones are gone, so we only meet the good ones." I watched Mr Rawat pause, fork halfway to his mouth. I don't know if he agreed. But later I heard him telling his neighbour about his brother's old scooter that broke down every week, which he'd clearly forgotten until then.

qa.a: Vidya smiled, called him Sir and asked a question instead of contradicting him, so Mr Rawat could think about it without losing face.

Wednesday. Leela spent her lunch break in the city archive, turning through old survey maps of the same lane. In 1900 there had been eleven houses. Only this wada was left. The others had been rebuilt, collapsed in floods, or pulled down long ago.
Friday. At the site meeting, Seema ma'am said it again. Leela said carefully, "Ma'am, I think we see the ones that were built best. The weak ones from that time aren't here for us to compare." Seema ma'am raised an eyebrow, then smiled a little. "Show me the maps."

Pallavi, you're rolling your eyes because Ramakant sir keeps saying machines were better in his day. Let me, Uday, tell you what I learned when I was twenty-five in this same textile mill.
My foreman then used to pat the oldest loom in the shed and say, "See this, boy? This one's from 1952. They built machines properly then. The new ones die in ten years."
I believed him. Then I was sent to clear the old store room. It was full of broken looms from the 1950s and 60s, dozens, rusted, cracked frames. Nobody talked about those. They'd been scrapped long ago.
The old loom in the shed was the one survivor out of many. Of course it looked like proof.
I never argued with him. But I stopped repeating it. Next time Ramakant sir says it, maybe just think of that store room.

qa.a: Broken looms from the 1950s and 60s, dozens, rusted, with cracked frames.

qa.q: Why did Uday believe the foreman at first?
qa.a: Uday felt convinced and impressed, since the 1952 loom was right there working, which seemed like proof, and the scrapped ones weren't visible anywhere.

qa.q: What does Uday suggest Pallavi do next time Ramakant sir talks about old machines?
qa.a: He suggests Pallavi just think of the store room full of scrapped looms, instead of eye-rolling or arguing.

qa.q: How might the foreman have seen the old loom compared with Uday later on?
qa.a: The foreman saw it as proof old machines were better built, while Uday came to see it as the one survivor of many that had failed.

passage: The site visit was running late, it was forty-two degrees, and the old contractor would not stop talking. "Look at that haveli across the street," he told Sangeeta ma'am, the senior architect. "Two hundred years and not one crack. Today's buildings fall down in twenty." Jagdish, the trainee, wiped his forehead and looked along the street. The haveli stood beautifully. But on either side were empty plots and one pile of old bricks where, the chaiwala said, houses from the same time had collapsed or been pulled down long ago. "Sir," Jagdish said, "maybe we only see the old ones that were strong. The weak ones aren't here any more." The contractor frowned. Sangeeta ma'am smiled for the first time that afternoon. "Write that down," she said. "We'll put it in the report."

qa.q: What was on either side of the haveli?
qa.a: Empty plots and one pile of old bricks.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he looked along the street?
qa.a: Jagdish was hot and tired but curious, noticing the empty plots and wondering what had happened to the other old houses.

qa.q: What did Jagdish point out, and why is it a fair correction?
qa.a: That only the strong old buildings still stand because the weak ones collapsed or were removed, so the survivors make old building look better than it was.

qa.q: How did the contractor react to Jagdish's point?
qa.a: The contractor frowned, probably not pleased to have his story questioned.

grounding: On a hot, rushed site visit, a young trainee notices that only the durable old buildings remain to be admired.

passage: At the family dinner in their Delhi flat, the radio played an old film song, and Pooja masi sighed. "They don't make music like this any more. Every song from our time was a gem. Today it's all noise." Varun, twenty-four, smiled and pulled up a list on his phone: every film song released in 1975. There were hundreds. He read a few titles aloud. Nobody at the table recognised them. "Masi, these are from your time too," he said. "We only hear the ones that were so good people kept playing them for fifty years. The rest disappeared." Pooja masi laughed and swatted his arm. "So you're saying my generation also made noise?" "Some. Just like mine. In fifty years, only our best will be left."

qa.q: Which year's film songs did Varun look up?
What does Varun's smile suggest as he pulls up the list?
qa.a: He felt amused and curious rather than annoyed, wanting to show Pooja masi the full picture gently.

qa.q: What point does Varun make, and why is it fair?

Lalremsiami tapped it. "It's lovely. But how many tiffins did your Nani's family buy in those fifty years?"
"I don't know. A few?"

Arohi turned the tiffin over, looking at the dents. "Nani did say she lost two on a train once."

passage: My grandfather likes to walk me past the old stone buildings near the fort in Jodhpur. "See? They built things to last back then. Now everything cracks in ten years," he says. I'm Ujjwal, and I'm an architect, so you'd think I'd argue. For a long time I didn't, because he seemed right. Then one afternoon, digging through the city archives for a project with my colleague Arohi, I found old survey maps from 1910. Hundreds of buildings were marked where there's nothing now. Mud-brick houses, cheap shops, badly built havelis. They fell down decades ago. The stone ones we see today are the survivors, the best of their time. The bad ones simply aren't there to compare. I still love walking with Dadaji. But now when he says "back then," I think about the maps.

qa.a: Old survey maps from 1910, with hundreds of buildings marked where there's nothing now.

Site note, heritage survey, old market, Kolkata. Week 3.
The caretaker, Ganga-di, told me again today, "They don't make buildings like this now." She means the arcade with the iron columns, and she's proud of it. It is beautiful. But I checked the municipal records this week. In 1930 this market had five arcades. Four were timber and brick, cheaply built, and burned or collapsed by the 1960s. Only this one, the most expensive, survived. So of course the survivor is well made. The weak ones aren't here to remind anyone.
I didn't argue with her. I asked if she remembered the other arcades. She did, one of them, a fire when she was small. She was quiet after that.
Next step: add a panel about the lost arcades to our report, so visitors see the whole picture.
Kiran

qa.a: Five arcades.

qa.q: How does Kiran seem to feel about Ganga-di's pride in the arcade?
qa.a: Kiran seems respectful and gentle, admiring the arcade too but uneasy about the claim, so Kiran asks a question instead of arguing.

qa.q: What is Kiran's next step, and why does it help?
qa.a: Adding a panel about the lost arcades to the report, so visitors see that the surviving arcade is not the whole picture.

qa.q: How might Ganga-di see the iron arcade after the conversation?
qa.a: She may still be proud of it, but, quiet and a little sad after remembering the fire, also see it as the lucky survivor among weaker buildings that were lost.

grounding: A young surveyor's note observes that old buildings seem better made because only the durable ones remain, while weaker ones have vanished.

passage:
Thursday.
Ramesh uncle came for dinner and did his usual speech. "Songs from the seventies were real music. Today's songs are rubbish." Papa nodded. I nodded too, to keep the peace.
But on the drive home I kept thinking. Ramesh uncle remembers maybe forty great songs from the seventies. The radio still plays them, so we all know them. What about the thousands of forgettable songs from then? They didn't survive. Nobody plays them, so nobody remembers they existed. Of course the old songs we hear sound better. We're hearing the best of ten years, and comparing it to everything from this one week.
I'm not going to lecture Ramesh uncle. But next time, I might ask him to name ten bad songs from 1975. I bet he can't.
Nirmal

passage:
In the village near Gangtok, Dolma had come home for the Losar holidays. At dinner, her uncle said again what he always said: "Old things were better. My grandfather's plough lasted fifty years. The new ones break in five."

Noor, Dolma's college friend visiting from Delhi, nodded politely.

Later, walking by the fields, Noor said, "Your uncle's plough story is interesting."

Dolma laughed. "I used to believe it too. But think: his grandfather probably had many ploughs. Some broke in a year. We only see the one that lasted fifty years because it's still here."

Noor thought. "So the old things that broke are gone. And we compare the one survivor to all the new ones."

"Exactly. Some new ploughs are bad. But the old weak ones aren't around to be counted."

Dolma didn't correct her uncle at dinner. But she smiled when he said it again.

qa.a: My grandfather's plough lasted fifty years.

qa.q: What does Dolma feel when her uncle repeats his story?
qa.a: Dolma feels fond and quietly amused, understanding why the story seems true but not needing to correct him.

qa.q: What insight did Dolma share with Noor?
qa.a: Dolma explained that only the surviving old plough is seen, while the old ones that broke are gone, so the comparison is unfair.

qa.q: How might Dolma's uncle feel if she explained this?
qa.a: The uncle might feel a bit challenged or amused, and may still prefer his memories of the old plough.

grounding: A young professional hears that old tools were better made and notes that only the durable ones remain to be seen.

passage:
Kaito had moved from Tokyo to work in Hanoi, and on weekends he explored the old quarter with his colleague Bao.

At a café, an old man at the next table said, "Buildings were made properly back then. Look at these colonial houses. A hundred years and still standing. The new towers crack in ten."

Bao nodded. "My grandmother says the same about songs. Old songs were all beautiful."

Kaito smiled. "But we only hear the old songs that people kept singing. The bad ones were forgotten long ago."

Bao thought. "And the buildings?"

"The weak houses from a hundred years ago collapsed or were torn down. We only see the strong ones."

"So we compare the best of the old to all of the new."

"Right. Some new towers are badly built. But the old weak ones aren't here to compare."

Bao laughed. "Don't tell my grandmother. She'll never forgive you."

qa.q: How long did the old man say the colonial houses had stood?
qa.a: A hundred years and still standing.

qa.q: What was Kaito feeling when the old man spoke?
qa.a: Kaito felt curious and a little amused, noticing that only the surviving old buildings and songs remain to be seen.

qa.q: What did Kaito's point about old songs help Bao see?
qa.a: It showed that people remember only the good old songs, just as only the strong old buildings remain, so comparisons with the new are unfair.

qa.q: How might Bao's grandmother feel hearing Kaito's view?
qa.a: Bao's grandmother might feel offended at first, since she loves the old songs and sees them as better.

grounding: A young professional abroad hears that old buildings were better made and notes that only the durable ones remain.
